items.headline: Amazon is in talks to buy Decart, the startup whose software moves AI work between rival chips, for about $7 billion
items.body: The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday, October 11, that Amazon is negotiating to acquire Decart, an Israeli-founded AI startup, for roughly $7 billion, citing people familiar with the talks; Decart was valued near $4 billion in a May round, per PitchBook data in the report. It builds software that lets developers shift AI workloads between different companies' chips, along with the video models Lucy and Oasis. Bloomberg reported that Anthropic examined buying Decart in August for as much as $6 billion and walked away after due diligence. Neither company has confirmed a deal.
items.plain: Running AI costs money mostly because of specialized chips, and nearly all of them come from one company, Nvidia. Decart writes the plumbing that lets a program built for Nvidia's chips run on a competitor's instead. Amazon makes its own AI chip, Trainium, and reportedly gave Decart early access to it. Buying the plumbing makes it easier for Amazon's customers to switch away from Nvidia, which is the point. Nothing is signed, so treat the price as reported rather than final.
items.why: Amazon would be paying roughly $7 billion not for a model but for the switching cost between chip vendors, which is the quietest chokepoint in the AI buildout.

items.headline: Trump announced a Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire; Zelenskyy says Russia kept bombing power plants
items.body: Trump said on Sunday, October 11, that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other's energy facilities. Zelenskyy told Axios the announcement “was news for me,” said Ukraine would agree if Russia did, and reported that Russian strikes hit Ukrainian power plants that same day, including in Kyiv and Kharkiv. On Monday he said the strikes had continued, according to the Washington Post. Moscow has not confirmed any agreement, and Trump made a similar announcement last month that neither party confirmed.
items.plain: Both sides have spent months bombing the other's power system — Ukraine hitting Russian oil refineries, Russia hitting Ukrainian power plants — which is one reason diesel and heating costs jumped worldwide. Trump said both had agreed to stop. Ukraine's president says nobody told him, and Russia has said nothing at all. Meanwhile Russian missiles hit Ukrainian plants the same day. So the ceasefire exists as an American announcement and not, so far, as anything either combatant has agreed to.
items.why: Brent crude fell about 1.5% on Monday partly on the ceasefire headline, which means a claim neither warring party has confirmed is now setting global fuel prices.

items.headline: The US emergency oil reserve sits at a 44-year low as the IEA prepares to release still more
items.body: The Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell to about 283.8 million barrels in late September, its lowest level since October 1982, after the US began delivering its 172-million-barrel share of the IEA's record 400-million-barrel March release and separately offered to loan 40 million barrels to energy companies. The Energy Department projects the reserve bottoming near 243 million barrels, and has estimated that refilling it to 680 million would cost about $20 billion. A Government Accountability Office report (GAO-26-106918) found that as of December 2025 the reserve's effective drawdown capability was 61% of its design rate and its fill capability 56%. The IEA's governing board meets Wednesday, October 15, to weigh further releases, with diesel the stated priority.
items.plain: The US stores crude oil in salt caverns along the Gulf Coast so it can flood the market with supply during a shortage. Two things have gone wrong at once. The caverns hold less oil than at any time since 1982, and the pumps and pipes that move it out can only run at about 61% of the speed they were built for. So the cushion is both thinner and slower to deploy. That matters now because diesel, the fuel that moves freight and runs farm equipment, is at record prices.
items.why: The tool governments reach for when fuel prices spike is being spent down just as diesel sets records, so the next shock arrives with less in reserve and a slower way to release it.

items.headline: The FDA approves the first new herpes antiviral mechanism in more than two decades
items.body: The FDA on Friday, October 9, approved Hovilpri (pritelivir) tablets, from Asahi Kasei, for immunocompromised adults whose herpes simplex virus lesions do not respond to acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir. Approval rested on Part C of the Phase 3 PRIOH-1 trial, a randomized, open-label study in 101 immunocompromised adults, in which about 63% of pritelivir patients had healed lesions by day 28 against 34% on the comparator, a difference of 28.7 percentage points (95% CI 8 to 47.1). Pritelivir is a helicase-primase inhibitor, a different mechanism from the nucleoside analogues that have defined HSV treatment since the 1980s.
items.plain: Herpes is normally controlled with acyclovir and its relatives, drugs that have been around for about forty years. In people whose immune systems are suppressed — transplant recipients, some cancer patients — the virus can mutate until those drugs stop working, and the fallback has been foscarnet, given by IV drip and hard on the kidneys. Pritelivir attacks a different part of the machinery the virus uses to copy itself, so resistance to the old drugs does not protect it, and it comes as a pill. The trial was open-label, meaning patients and doctors knew who got which drug, which makes the healing numbers less airtight than a blinded trial's would be.
items.why: Moving a drug-resistant infection from an IV infusion with kidney toxicity to an oral tablet changes where those patients get treated, not just what they take.

items.headline: Houthis strike Riyadh's main airport a second day as Yemeni government forces claim the Bab al-Mandeb strait
items.body: Saudi authorities said an “unidentified projectile” struck a passenger terminal at King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, October 11, starting a fire and causing injuries, a day after a Houthi missile strike on the same airport killed 12 and wounded 309. The Houthis claimed the Sunday attack; Saudi Arabia said it would respond “decisively,” and Trump said the US is evaluating whether to join the Saudi-backed offensive. Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces said they had taken control of Bab al-Mandeb and begun a “strategic offensive operation” toward Sanaa, claims the Houthi-run Saba agency called “fictitious.”
items.plain: Bab al-Mandeb is the narrow gate between the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean, and every ship heading for the Suez Canal has to pass through it. Yemen's internationally recognized government, backed by Saudi Arabia, says it has taken that gate from the Houthis, who have spent years using the coastline to threaten shipping. The Houthis say the claim is invented, and no outside party has verified it. What is confirmed is that Riyadh's main airport has now been hit on consecutive days, which is why Saudi Arabia is pressing Washington to join in.
items.why: Whoever holds Bab al-Mandeb sets the insurance rate on Suez-bound shipping, so a contested claim about a few kilometres of Yemeni coast is also a global freight-cost story.

items.headline: North Korea fires several ballistic missiles, then denies it, days after Seoul revealed a hypersonic test
items.body: South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected several ballistic missiles launched from the Pyongyang area at about 9:20 a.m. local time on Monday, October 12, flying toward the East Sea, with one estimated at more than 900 km; Japan's defence ministry confirmed at least one suspected ballistic missile. South Korea's National Security Office convened an emergency meeting. SBS reported it was the 16th such launch this year, and analysts tied it to Seoul's disclosure four days earlier of a hypersonic glide vehicle test. UPI reported that Pyongyang denied responsibility and accused Seoul of fabricating its findings.
items.plain: A hypersonic glide vehicle is a warhead that flies low and changes course on the way down, which makes it much harder to shoot down; South Korea said four days ago that it had tested one. North Korea answered with missiles of its own, fired into the sea rather than at anything. The denial is the strange part. North Korea normally publicizes its launches as a show of strength, and this time it says Seoul made the detection up, even though Japan tracked a missile too.
items.why: Each Korea is now testing to answer the other's test, which shortens the gap between demonstrations and removes the quiet stretches that used to leave room for talks.

items.headline: US measles cases reach 4,080, the country's worst year since 1991
items.body: The CDC had confirmed 4,080 measles cases in 2026 as of October 8, up 193 in a week, with 414 hospitalizations, about 10% of cases, and 95% of cases in people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown. The CDC has confirmed two measles deaths this year, while Pennsylvania alone reports five, according to Becker's Hospital Review. The Pan American Health Organization's measles commission will review whether the US keeps its measles elimination status at its annual meeting in November, a review postponed from April.
items.plain: Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, meaning it no longer spread continuously here: imported cases burned out fast because almost everyone around them was vaccinated. A country loses that status if a single chain of transmission runs for more than twelve months. That is what PAHO will decide in November, by checking whether the outbreak that began in West Texas is genetically linked to later ones. The 95% figure is the whole mechanism in one number — this is not a vaccine that stopped working, it is a vaccine fewer people are taking.
items.why: Losing elimination status would be the first reversal of a US disease-elimination milestone, and it turns on a committee reading transmission chains rather than on the case count itself.

items.headline: Robert Hall and Michael Woodford win the economics Nobel for the theory underneath modern central banking
items.body: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the 2026 Prize in Economic Sciences on Monday, October 12, to Robert E. Hall of Stanford and Michael Woodford of Columbia for work on the microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization. The academy said their models are the basis for smoothing out booms and busts, and that well-timed fiscal and monetary measures can reduce an economy's peaks and troughs. Each receives 6 million Swedish kronor, about $598,000. It was the last of this year's prizes.
items.plain: Economies swing between booms and slumps, and central banks try to damp the swings by moving interest rates. For a long time that was largely rules of thumb. Hall and Woodford built the mathematics underneath it, showing how millions of separate decisions about prices, wages and hiring add up to the behaviour of a whole economy, and therefore which policy move works and when. Woodford's work in particular is why central banks now announce what they intend to do next instead of simply doing it: what people expect is itself part of the mechanism.
items.why: The prize lands two days before the September inflation print and about two weeks before an October 28 Fed decision, with headline inflation last measured at 3.4% in August.

items.headline: Ledger confirms a hidden implant inside a hardware wallet sold by a reseller, with analysts tracing about $93 million drained
items.body: Ledger said on October 10 that one of its hardware wallets sold through the Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis contained an unauthorized hardware implant. Blockchain analytics firm Bitquery traced about $92.9 million drained from 311 wallets across five chains; Ledger has not verified that figure or established that the implant caused the thefts, and other analysts put losses above $72 million. Researchers including former Mt. Gox chief Mark Karpelès describe a concealed board able to read the 24-word recovery phrase off the screen during setup and transmit it over a cellular connection. Ledger said it has “no indication that Ledger's security infrastructure, systems or services have been compromised,” and told anyone who bought from CryptoBilis in the past 90 days not to initialize an unused device. CryptoBilis has halted all hardware wallet sales.
items.plain: A hardware wallet is a small offline device that holds the secret phrase controlling your cryptocurrency, and the entire point is that the phrase never touches an internet-connected computer. Someone appears to have opened these devices before they were sold and added a chip that reads the phrase off the screen during setup and sends it away over a mobile network. That defeats the design without breaking any of its cryptography, because the attack happens before the owner ever opens the box. Ledger's built-in “genuine check” tests the device's software, not whether the case was opened, so it would not catch this.
items.why: This is a supply-chain attack on the one object people buy specifically to avoid trusting anyone else's computer, and the only defence is physical custody of the box, which no software update can provide.

items.headline: A judge orders the administration to pull TV ads featuring Trump after $19 million of the $20 million was already spent
items.body: Judge Jennifer L. Rochon of the Southern District of New York granted a two-week temporary restraining order on Sunday, October 11, barring the administration from using funds appropriated to the Department of Homeland Security to “develop, create, disseminate, place, distribute, publish, or air the challenged advertisements,” and requiring cancellation of spots scheduled from Sunday night onward. DHS set aside about $20 million through Customs and Border Protection; a sworn declaration from a DHS official said the contractor, LMD Agency, had already purchased media buys “at an approximate cost of $19,000,000.” Rochon found the plaintiffs — a coalition including Common Cause and SEIU Local 32BJ — “likely to succeed on the merits,” and rejected the Justice Department's argument that the case was moot because the ads “will not continue past tomorrow.” The White House said the spots were public service announcements and that Trump would not reimburse the government for ads already aired; Trump said future ads would be paid for by his political committee. The order is temporary and is not a final ruling that the ads were illegal.
items.plain: Congress hands agencies money for named purposes, and a long-standing clause in those spending bills bars using it for “publicity or propaganda” inside the United States. The suit says Homeland Security used border-enforcement money to run commercials featuring the president a few weeks before the midterm elections. The judge has not decided that question; she stopped the ads while she considers it, which is a lower bar to clear. The detail that does the work is the $19 million out of $20 million: by the time the order arrived, the money was already committed, and the White House has said it will not be paid back.
items.why: The order stops future spending but cannot recover what was already committed, which makes the remaining fight about whether an administration can spend an appropriation first and litigate it afterward.
